name: farkle-r3
context:
ROUND 3. Both your findings are accepted, and the fix for the first one produced a result that also answers the second. Everything below is measured on the real Farkle scoring table with exhaustive path enumeration.

─────────── (a) THE FOUR RISK-FREE STEPS WERE PADDING. YOU WERE RIGHT. ───────────

You wrote: 'they are not playing during those steps; they are merely collecting... you haven't built a game; you've built a loading bar that eventually turns into a game.' Accepted without reservation.

The diagnosis was that the board must be TIGHT FROM STEP ONE. So the turn no longer operates on all 36 cells. It operates on a LIVE HAND — a connected region drawn at turn start — which is the direct analogue of rolling six dice rather than owning the table.

I then had to pick the hand size, and rather than choose one I swept it against a target I did not invent: the REAL TABLETOP FARKLE CURVE, computed by brute force over 200,000 throws per depth, every subset tested for a score:

    6 dice 2.3%   5 dice 7.8%   4 dice 15.8%   3 dice 27.8%   2 dice 44.3%   1 die 66.8%

Sweeping live-hand size on the grid, the RMS distance from that curve falls monotonically from 55.0 at hand 6 to 7.5 at hand 20. Hand 6 collapses in three steps — adjacency fragments a small blob instantly, which tabletop does not suffer because set-aside dice leave no holes behind.

─────────── THE RESULT THAT MATTERS, AND IT ANSWERS (e) TOO ───────────

While sweeping I noticed the grid curve was always CONVEX — flat, then a cliff — where the tabletop curve is smooth. I suspected my agent rather than the design: it always took the maximum-scoring path, which is usually the full six cells, whereas a tabletop player sets aside one or two dice.

Tested directly. Hand of 16, same 2000 boards, three policies:

    policy      step1 step2 step3 step4 step5 step6   cells/step   RMS vs tabletop
    MAXSCORE     0.0   0.7  15.7  45.7  69.0  86.8       3.02          15.2
    FEWEST       0.0   0.0   0.5   4.8  11.4  26.2       1.37          24.4
    EFFICIENT    0.0   0.7  10.1  27.5  44.0  60.1       2.52           4.7
    TABLETOP     2.3   7.8  15.8  27.8  44.3  66.8

Two things fall out.

FIRST, EFFICIENT PLAY REPRODUCES THE TABLETOP CURVE. RMS 4.7 across six depths, with no parameter fitted to it — the only knob was hand size, chosen before this comparison. The design has the tabletop feel for a player who plays well, and that is not an assertion, it is a distance.

SECOND, AND THIS IS THE ANSWER TO YOUR CALCULATOR PROBLEM: THE RISK CURVE IS NOT A PROPERTY OF THE DESIGN. IT IS A CONSEQUENCE OF THE PLAYER'S POLICY. The same board at the same step is 0.5% lethal to one policy and 15.7% to another. There is no fixed schedule to read off a strip, because the strip cannot know how fast the player intends to burn the board. You wrote that 'there must remain a gap between the mathematically correct move and the human move'; the gap here is that risk is endogenous — it is caused by the choice, not surveyed before it.

So idea 55 is amended rather than dropped. Row 2 does not show a probability. It shows the risk THE CURRENTLY-TRACED CHAIN WOULD LEAVE BEHIND, quantised to the four nameable states the strip already uses — a claim about the consequence of this move, not a forecast of the turn. It updates as the player drags, it is explicitly a UV-3 synthetic claim, and like every claim in this project it is allowed to be wrong.

─────────── ONE THING I WILL NOT CLAIM ───────────

In the table above FEWEST reaches the highest mean turn score. That looks like the dominant degenerate strategy you predicted, and I am NOT reporting it as one, because my probe has no banking decision — the policies play until death and a farkle zeroes the run, so FEWEST wins by surviving rather than by scoring. Without bank-aware agents the comparison is an artifact of the probe. It becomes the first question the Monte Carlo harness answers, with RANDOM, GREEDY, EFFICIENT and a bank-aware search agent over identical seed batteries, reporting the SPREAD rather than the mean.

─────────── WHAT IS NOW FIXED ───────────

58 The turn operates on a LIVE HAND of 16 connected cells drawn at turn start, not the whole board. 59 Hand size is 16 because a sweep put it nearest the real tabletop curve, and if the scoring table changes the sweep must be re-run. 60 Cleared cells do not refill inside a turn. 61 Refill and gravity happen between turns, from the draw-ordinal stream, so the forecast strip is unchanged. 62 Row 2 shows the risk the traced chain would LEAVE, in four states, updating as the player drags. 63 The Monte Carlo gate reports per-step farkle frequency, never pooled, because pooling averages a 0% region against a 90% one.

CARRIED FROM ROUND 2: wildcards stay cut; coop is a shared board with separate banks; the pay table is published and combos are named; the preview and the executor share one scoring path.

CARRIED FROM ROUND 1: pip tokens through the existing 4D projection, amber identity axis against chemistry's cyan and darkmatter's magenta, chain drawn as a ribbon, bombs earned by named combos only, solo/vs/coop on one executor, VS on a shared seed with blind settlement.

questions.text: Efficient play lands within RMS 4.7 of the real tabletop risk curve with only hand size as a free parameter. Is matching the tabletop curve actually the right target for a grid game, or have I optimised toward a feel that the grid should be free to differ from?

Risk is endogenous — caused by the player's own chain choice rather than surveyed in advance. Does that genuinely dissolve the Calculator Problem you raised, or does it just relocate the calculation to a per-chain one the UI will end up doing anyway?
I refused to call FEWEST a dominant strategy because my probe lacks a banking decision. Is that the correct restraint, or am I declining to report a finding that is already visible in the numbers?
A live hand of 16 connected cells inside a 36-cell board leaves 20 cells visible but untouchable this turn. Does that read as a rule a player will understand, or as an arbitrary fence?
Is this design now ready to build, or name the one thing that must be settled first.
